traversal_accounting_correction.correction: b_t(e) is an aggregate per-token-edge integer counting pairs of excess traversal incidences. It is not an integer contribution attached canonically to an individual swap. A swap may contain zero, one, or two excess traversal incidences; only the aggregate equation s(e)-r(e)=sum_t b_t(e) follows.

example.verification: The first and third x-m swaps each contain one baseline and one excess traversal incidence. Together these are two excess incidences, or 2*b_M(xm), while the aggregate excess-swap count is one.

double_star_theorem.status: independently_reproved; no counterexample or proof gap found
double_star_theorem.class: Finite tree with adjacent centers u,v, arbitrary pendant leaf sets L,R (possibly empty), and a bijective token-to-vertex destination map.
double_star_theorem.claim: Deterministic O(n)-time matching-round schedule with R <= 2r+2max(a,b)=2max(W(u),W(v))<=2*LB_hub<=2*OPT.
proof_checks: Bijective cut balance gives r outward tokens in each direction across the central edge.
If a center lacks an outgoing token while its side has positive remaining demand, an outgoing token lies on an incident leaf.
After preparation and a bridge swap, each side's outgoing count decreases by one; induction reaches zero without stranding a token.
A prepared leaf receives a locally destined center token and is never outgoing again; initially correct leaves are not selected.
Center-containing cycles sort in q center swaps; leaf-only q-cycles sort in q+1<=2q swaps; fixed points are skipped.
Within-star swaps are serialized; the disjoint left and right star sequences run in lockstep as matchings.
Phase I costs <=2r, Phase II <=2max(a,b), and W(u)=r+a, W(v)=r+b.
Identity and two-vertex degenerate cases are covered; output has O(n) rounds and swaps.
double_star_theorem.scope: This theorem is complete for double-stars only. It proves no result for three or more hubs or arbitrary trees.
double_star_theorem.independent_review: passed; reconstructed cut invariant, token identities, leaf non-reuse, cycle words, matching legality, total bound, and running time from first principles

prior_art_audit.publication_assessment: Retain as a correct restricted-class theorem/algorithmic corollary. It is not presently a credible standalone paper contribution: the single-cut decomposition is elementary, star-transposition words are classical, and the result has no broader structural principle beyond double-stars. A publishable direction would require a nontrivial instance-sensitive theorem for unboundedly many interacting hubs or a sharp exact double-star characterization.

Roberts_Symvonis_Zhang_1995.scope_analysis: These are offline worst-case routing-number bounds in the matching model. General double-stars have unbounded center degrees, so the degree-3 case does not cover them except bounded tiny cases. The arbitrary-tree O(n) statement covers the host but is not instance-sensitive in LB_hub and does not directly imply R<=2*LB_hub. No diameter-three-specific statement appears in the publisher theorem summary.

Zhang_1999.published_guarantee: rt(T)<=3n/2+O(log n) for every n-vertex tree
Zhang_1999.scope_analysis: Broader graph-class coverage, still a worst-case-in-n statement; does not directly imply the fixed-permutation 2*LB_hub guarantee.

theorem_level_comparison.nonimplication_witness_to_naive_size_arg: A double-star may have arbitrarily many leaves while a permutation moves only two leaves, for which LB_hub=2. Therefore an O(n) routing-number bound alone cannot yield R<=2*LB_hub. This distinguishes theorem forms; it does not rule out deriving a result using additional instance reduction.

sources.citation: Roberts, Symvonis, Zhang (1995), Routing on Trees via Matchings
sources.comparison: Publisher states worst-case bounds rt(T)<=2n for maximum-degree-3 trees, <=2n+o(n) for bounded-degree trees, and <=13n/5 for arbitrary trees. A general double-star may have unbounded degree. These bounds depend on n and do not directly give the permutation-specific 2*LB_hub guarantee.

sources.citation: Alon, Chung, Graham (1994), Routing Permutations on Graphs via Matchings
sources.comparison: Same matching-round model; worst-case routing number, not this instance-wise double-star LB_hub guarantee.

sources.citation: Zhang (1999), Optimal Bounds for Matching Routing on Trees
sources.comparison: Worst-case 3n/2+O(log n) bound for arbitrary n-node trees; incomparable with the instance-relative double-star bound.

sources.citation: Aichholzer et al. (ESA 2022), Hardness of Token Swapping on Trees
sources.comparison: Parallel matching-round PTS is NP-complete on trees; hardness is not an approximation lower bound and does not imply this restricted guarantee.

sources.citation: Bansal, Günlük, Shapley (2025 version), Parallel Token Swapping for Qubit Routing
sources.comparison: Constant-factor approximations for cycles, subdivided stars and grids; genuine double-stars with both branching centers are outside the one-junction subdivided-star class.

sources.citation: Sadanandan, Chitturi (2022), Optimal Algorithms for Sorting Permutations with Brooms
sources.comparison: Optimal sequential swap count on broom/double-broom classes, not parallel matching-round makespan.

sources.citation: Irving, Rattan (2009), Minimal Factorizations of Permutations into Star Transpositions
sources.comparison: Classical context for local star cycle words; no double-star matching schedule result.

prior_art_audit.audit_boundary: Targeted theorem-level comparison of primary sources, including the Springer publisher statement for Roberts-Symvonis-Zhang; not an exhaustive literature search or proof of firstness. The result is no direct implication found, not global absence.
